THE DAILY METALS PULSE ⚡ | TUESDAY CLOSE • NOV 24, 2026
#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

This morning I asked whether silver could reclaim $43 and gold could hold $3,600. By the COMEX settlement, silver was closer to $40 than $43, and gold had given back nearly $90 an ounce.

🥈 Silver took the hardest hit. November futures settled at $40.76/oz, down 5.5%, erasing Monday’s entire gain. Gold settled at $3,559.90/oz, down 2.4%. Gold held on to about a third of Monday’s rebound. Silver gave back every cent and another $0.28.

🔌 Copper followed silver. Shanghai’s overnight rally had been driven largely by traders covering shorts. By the New York settlement, December copper had fallen nearly 5%, more than wiping out Monday’s 2.7% gain.

☢️ One number puts the U.S. uranium supply story in perspective. Eight facilities produced uranium in Q3, yet total U.S. concentrate output fell 78% from Q2 to just 243,673 lb. The main reason was that Energy Fuels paused uranium processing at White Mesa to rebuild its ore inventory. Its next mill run targets roughly 1 million lb starting in December. That single run would produce more than four times what the entire country turned out in Q3.

🇺🇸 U.S. consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 from 91.9. The $70 billion five-year Treasury auction drew slightly softer demand, with a yield of 4.719% against 4.717% just before the sale. That was a small miss for bonds on a brutal day for metals.

Tomorrow at 8:30 a.m. ET, October PCE inflation and the revised Q3 GDP figure land together. I’m watching silver’s reaction to a softer inflation reading in particular. If yields fall and silver still struggles to hold $40, that would tell me sellers have more to unload.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the next Daily Metals Pulse.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Every good exit is a reason to celebrate, but some are a bit more special than others.

The sale of my Nanotyrannus Jodi for $47.3 million some weeks ago is one of these special ones. 

Fun fact: Jodi was originally named Chomper, until potential copyright issues forced us to find a new name – making Jodi the first gender-fluid dino. 😉

Several bidders battled for more than twelve minutes at Sotheby’s in New York, driving Jodi’s price to more than five times its high estimate and making it the second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction, behind only Gus, the T. rex that fetched $50.1 million in July.

With this sale, my investment firm @ApeironInvests has not only generated exceptional returns but also demonstrated once more our recurring ability to identify and pioneer entirely new asset classes and investment themes.

We were among the first professional investors to recognize the potential of dinosaur fossils,appreciating not only their extraordinary beauty and scientific significance, but also their economic value.

As for Jodi, I believe the outcome is well deserved. Jodi is an exceptionally rare mounted Nanotyrannus skeleton, one of only three such substantial specimens known to science.

I am particularly proud that Jodi has also contributed to advancing scientific knowledge about dinosaurs, especially the tyrannosaur family. For more than 80 years, paleontologists debated whether smaller tyrannosaurid skeletons like Jodi belonged to juvenile T. rex or represented a separate genus.

Last fall, that debate took a major turn with the publication of a groundbreaking paper in Nature demonstrating that Nanotyrannus is indeed a valid genus that coexisted with T. rex at the end of the Cretaceous, occupying its own distinct ecological niche. Eighty-four years after the discovery of the type specimen, the scientific conversation around Nanotyrannus has fundamentally shifted, making it one of the most exciting developments in paleontology in recent decades.

Standing approximately 9 feet 6 inches tall on its armature and measuring 19.6 feet from nose to tail (about 2.9 by 6 meters), Jodi was the first Nanotyrannus to come to market following last fall's landmark scientific development.

We have plenty more extraordinary dinosaur fossils in our collection, so stay tuned to discover more about Apeiron’s prehistoric division.

On Sunday, OpenAI's chief scientist called the thing his company builds "an alien mind" and asked rival labs to agree on a speed limit for it. A few hours later, Meta's chief AI officer used nearly the same words about the Claude-assisted Riemann proof, "completed with the help of an alien mind that we don't understand," and declared that superintelligence is arriving.

In between, Elon Musk posted to 53,000 likes: "Consciousness is either an illusion or ubiquitous on a gradient. Difficult to argue that carbon is conscious, but silicon is not." Meanwhile, the proof that set off the weekend has been certified by software, is roughly 250,000 pages long by one estimate, and the Clay Institute still lists the problem as unsolved.

So by Sunday night the industry agreed the machine is alien, possibly conscious, better at math than anyone alive, and in need of a cap.

Philosophers spent 2,500 years asking what a mind is. OpenAI answered with a number, then asked everyone to promise not to make it any smaller.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
BEFORE IT WAS OBVIOUS: @coinbase. You can be wrong about the market and right about the founder.

@TimDraper almost missed Coinbase.

In his account, @brian_armstrong originally pitched Coinbase to Joel Yarmon and Tim. Draper liked Armstrong, but the firm had already invested in CoinLab, a Bitcoin exchange focused on institutional investors. They made a strategic judgment: Coinbase was going after retail consumers, and they thought that route would take too long. So Draper passed.

His son @AdamDraper saw it differently. Adam Draper met Brian separately and wrote Coinbase his first check. Then the market started answering the question.

Coinbase grew, consumer adoption accelerated. Crypto moved far beyond the relatively small audience that existed when the company was founded. And when Coinbase raised another round, Draper Associates invested. Tim writes that the Coinbase investment ultimately returned nearly twice the size of an entire Draper Associates fund.

There’s an important lesson buried in the part of the story where they were initially wrong. The team correctly recognized Brian Armstrong as exceptional, but underestimated the path he had chosen.

Why it matters for builders: investors can be wrong about your market timing, your customer, or even your entire strategy while still recognizing something unusual in you. And investors should remember the inverse: sometimes the unconventional go-to-market strategy is exactly what creates the enormous market.

Retail crypto looked like the longer road, yet it became the road to mass adoption.

This is excellent. I increasingly think reality is the ultimate verifier and time and money are its two best reward signals aka how well can you predict the future. 

If we ever achieve real superintelligence, I think its most impressive capability won’t be solving math problems or writing code but its ability to predict the future with decent accuracy. Predicting reality across economics, geopolitics, biology, technology etc requires an incredibly deep understanding of how the world works and how everything interacts.

What I love about prediction markets as an RL environment is that you get an infinite stream of new, uncontaminated problems. Time reveals the ground truth and money gives you a quantitative reward signal. You can’t fake dollars. 

Maybe the ultimate benchmark for AGI is simply how well it can predict a world that doesn’t exist yet.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Announcing Epochal! ✨

We believe the best measure of intelligence is the ability to predict the future. Doing so requires learning about the past and constantly working to be less wrong.

Today's AI has read almost everything and lived through almost nothing. It learns from the internet all at once, already knowing how each story ends. 

We want it to live through thousands of yesterdays instead, one day at a time, the way people do.

So, we built Epochal Time Portal, the first true point-in-time environment with trillions of pages spanning 30 years of history, where agents can browse the Internet as it existed on a past date.

I just realized that the 20th century was perhaps an anomaly in how much it rewarded being book smart over street smart. For 80 years, the recipe for success was to study hard, get a degree, specialize and follow the rules. AI is about to commoditize much of what made that recipe work.

I think we’re entering an era that will disproportionately reward the curious, the resourceful, the self-taught and those who thrive in uncertainty. When intelligence becomes abundant, agency becomes scarce. That’s probably the most important thing we can cultivate in our kids now.

@NaveenGRao sold Nervana to Intel and MosaicML to Databricks. His third company, @unconvai, is building something that looks nothing like a GPU.

His argument: AI is now limited by energy, so the number that matters is joules per token. Getting there means dropping the von Neumann split between memory and compute and building a machine that is "programmed by weights."

To learn fast, they tape out a new chip roughly every three months. Their first test chip, a system of coupled oscillators, generated small images at about 900 nanojoules each, against about 50 millijoules on a GPU.

@dylan522p asks why so many analog chips blew their lead once you count the conversion costs, whether programmability still matters when NVIDIA is king, and whether we will stop buying computers and start buying intelligence tokens.

Tape Out is a new SemiAnalysis series with the founders building AI hardware. This is episode one.

Now that official results are out, we see that AMD’s Venice competes very well with NVIDIA’s Vera CPU in per-thread performance in SPEC CPU 2026 intrate. The flagship 256-core EPYC 9996 comes close despite running at less than half the power per core, while Venice-HF is 26-38% faster than Vera thanks to 60% higher clockspeeds. Discounting stockfish, Venice-HF is still 21-33% faster. Even in agentic and EDA tasks which Vera excels at, Venice-HF is still 11-21% faster on a per-thread basis.

AMD results from official SPECrate®2026_int_base (n-copy) 2P SMT submissions compiled with GCC 16 with amdalloc and amdlibm AOCC 6.0 libraries. Estimated results without fine tuning will be lower.
